title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS), a chronic musculoskeletal pain condition characterized by localized or regional pain, taut bands, and myofascial trigger points.
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle to situate fascia within a multifactorial framework, but never defines the model. It lists biological (fascial pathology), psychological (stress, catastrophizing, maladaptive coping), and social (inactivity) factors in parallel without specifying mechanisms linking them, and the social domain is minimal.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fascial pathology generates nociceptive input leading to central sensitization (bio-psych directional). Psychological and social factors (stress, catastrophizing, inactivity) are asserted to amplify pain via neuroimmune pathways, but no specific mechanism is detailed. No three-domain mechanism is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims a biopsychosocial framework but provides minimal social content (only 'inactivity' is named) and no definition of the BPS model
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological factors (fascial pathology) are elaborated in detail, while psychological factors are only named and social factors are nearly absent, creating an imbalance
conceptual_tensions_3: The paper lists biological, psychological, and social factors in parallel without specifying how they interact mechanistically, despite claiming an integrative model
additional_observations_1: The paper introduces a novel 'fascial-neurogenic route' as a distinct etiopathophysiological pathway alongside the traditional 'myogenic route', but does not integrate these with psychosocial factors
additional_observations_2: The paper uses the term 'biopsychosocial' as an organizing principle but never defines what the model means, and the social domain is limited to a single factor ('inactivity')
synthesis_note: This narrative review elaborates biological mechanisms of fascial pathology in myofascial pain syndrome but uses the biopsychosocial label as an organizing principle without defining the model. Psychological factors are named but not defined, and social content is minimal. Integration is partial: biological and psychological domains are directionally linked via central sensitization, but no three-domain mechanism is proposed.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS language is used but social domain is minimal and psychological constructs are only named. Triadic integration is partial because bio-psych is directional but social is only mentioned alongside. Bio-dominant balance reflects the paper's focus on fascial mechanisms.

title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS), described as localized or regional pain with taut bands and myofascial trigger points reproducing referred pain when palpated.
context_note: Paper references the general population, specialized pain clinics, chronic low back and neck pain, and international initiatives for consensus terminology.
bps_function_set: explanatory framework; intervention rationale; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS mainly as an organizing and explanatory frame for a fascia-centered MPS model. It lists fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial factors, then links some through peripheral input, central sensitization, neuroimmune pathways, and multimodal treatment. It does not provide formal BPS definitions or operationalized variables.
integration_mechanism_summary: The main mechanism is peripheral-to-central: fascial densification, fibrosis, and inflammation generate nociceptive input, which contributes to peripheral sensitization, central sensitization, dorsal horn hyperexcitability, descending control changes, and cortical reorganization. Psychosocial factors are said to amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways, but no detailed psychosocial mechanism is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_1: sanra (scale for the assessment of narrative review articles)
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper argues for fascia as a central peripheral driver while also insisting that fascia should not be viewed in isolation
conceptual_tensions_2: It uses a biopsychosocial frame but gives much more substantive attention to fascia and central sensitization than to social factors
conceptual_tensions_3: It proposes psychosocial factors amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways but does not elaborate the psychosocial mechanism
conceptual_tensions_4: It criticizes muscle-centric and central sensitization models as incomplete, while proposing fascia as a unifying substrate that may risk reductionism if psychosocial domains are ignored
additional_observations_1: The article is a conceptual narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, despite searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar
additional_observations_2: The review's most concrete operationalization is a named integrative conceptual model with fascial pathology, muscular dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial influences
additional_observations_3: Psychological and social constructs are named but not measured, defined, or linked to specific instruments
additional_observations_4: The social domain is essentially collapsed into psychosocial factors, with no named social determinants such as work, family, healthcare access, or socioeconomic position
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a fascia-centered explanatory frame for MPS. Biological content is rich and sustained, especially fascia, nociception, inflammation, mechanotransduction, and central sensitization. Psychological content is present but mostly listed and undifferentiated. Social content is thin and underexplored. The paper proposes peripheral-to-central and neuroimmune pathways, but triadic integration remains partial rather than a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS is used analytically to organize fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial content, but social factors are minimally specified and triadic integration is mostly parallel with some peripheral-to-central mechanisms.

title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS by integrating fascial pathology with muscle dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial factors into a conceptual model that explains MPS heterogeneity and guides multimodal treatment.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that fascial pathology generates nociceptive input that drives central sensitization, while psychological stress amplifies pain through neuroimmune pathways. All three domains form a descriptive integrative model without specified mechanistic pathways.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between fascia-focused biological model and incomplete integration of psychosocial domain
conceptual_tensions_2: Tension between historical muscle-centric models and emerging fascial mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_3: Tension between descriptive triadic integration and lack of specified mechanistic pathways
additional_observations_1: The paper uses BPS terminology extensively but primarily develops the biological domain with fascial mechanisms
additional_observations_2: Psychological and social factors are mentioned but not elaborated with specific constructs or measures
additional_observations_3: The integrative model is presented descriptively rather than through specified mechanistic pathways
additional_observations_4: The paper acknowledges its own limitations in psychosocial domain coverage
synthesis_note: This paper operationalizes the biopsychosocial model by integrating fascial pathology with muscle dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial factors into a conceptual model for MPS. While the biological domain is elaborately developed with fascial mechanisms, psychological and social domains are minimally covered. The integration is descriptive rather than mechanistic, with fascial pathology positioned as a peripheral driver that interacts with central and psychosocial factors. The paper acknowledges gaps in psychosocial integration and terminology standardization.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is multifactorial because all three domains are present but biological domain is elaborated while others are mentioned. Triadic integration is descriptive because all domains are related but no mechanistic pathways are specified. Biological coverage is elaborated due to detailed fascial mechanisms; psychological and social are mentioned due to brief references to stress and inactivity.
